cards.title: Introduction to Streams
cards.content:
What is a Stream?

Introduced in Java 8, the java.util.stream package provides a declarative API to process collections of elements.

Unlike collections, a stream is not a data structure that stores elements. Instead, it conveys elements from a source (such as a Collection, an Array, or an I/O channel) through a pipeline of computational steps.

Key Characteristics:

  • No Storage: A stream doesn't hold data; it processes data on demand.
  • Functional in Nature: Operations on a stream produce a result but do not modify its source.
  • Laziness-oriented: Many stream operations (like filtering) can be deferred and computed only when necessary.

cards.title: How to Create Streams
cards.content:
Creating Streams in Java

There are several ways to instantiate a Stream depending on your data source:

1. From Collections

List<String> names = List.of("Alice", "Bob");
Stream<String> stream = names.stream();

2. From Arrays

String[] arr = {"a", "b", "c"};
Stream<String> streamOfArray = Arrays.stream(arr);

3. Using Static Factory Methods

Stream<Integer> directStream = Stream.of(1, 2, 3);

cards.title: Intermediate Operations
cards.content:
Transforming and Filtering Streams

Intermediate operations return a new Stream and are lazy (not executed until a terminal operation runs).

Common Intermediate Operations:

  • filter(Predicate): Discards elements that don't match the condition.
  • map(Function): Transforms each element into another object.
  • sorted(): Returns a sorted view of the stream.
  • distinct(): Removes duplicate elements.

Example pipeline:

names.stream()
     .filter(name -> name.startsWith("A"))
     .map(String::toUpperCase);

cards.title: Terminal Operations
cards.content:
Closing the Pipeline

Terminal operations trigger the stream pipeline execution and produce a final non-stream result (like a List, Map, single value, or void).

Common Terminal Operations:

  • forEach(Consumer): Performs an action for each element.
  • collect(Collector): Accumulates elements into a collection.
  • reduce(BinaryOperator): Combines stream elements into a single summary value.
  • count(): Returns the number of elements.

Note: Once a terminal operation completes, the stream is considered consumed and cannot be reused.

cards.title: The Power of Lazy Evaluation
cards.content:
Understanding Laziness

In Java, intermediate operations are not evaluated instantly. They construct a recipe of execution paths instead.

Consider this example:

Stream.of("one", "two", "three")
      .filter(s -> {
          System.out.println("Filtering: " + s);
          return s.length() > 3;
      });

If you execute this code, nothing is printed! Because there is no terminal operation, the filter block is never evaluated. This optimization allows Java to minimize iterations over data.

cards.title: Parallel Streams
cards.content:
Scaling Up with Parallel Processing

Java Streams make concurrency accessible by letting you parallelize calculations effortlessly using parallelStream().

Under the hood, parallel streams utilize the ForkJoinPool.commonPool() to distribute chunks of data across CPU cores.

When to Use:

  • Large datasets.
  • CPU-intensive operations.
  • Stateless, independent computations (avoid shared mutable state!).
List<Integer> numbers = List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5);
numbers.parallelStream()
       .map(n -> n * 2)
       .forEach(System.out::println);

cards.title: Stream Best Practices
cards.content:
Write Clean, Safe Stream Pipelines

Follow these rules of thumb to write maintainable Java Streams:

1. Do Not Re-Use Streams

Once a terminal operation is called, the stream is closed. Accessing it again throws an IllegalStateException.

2. Avoid Side Effects in Lambdas

Lambdas inside stream operations should be stateless and non-interfering. Avoid mutating outside variables from within map/filter blocks.

3. Keep it Readable

Avoid massive, nested, or overly complex stream pipelines. If a stream is unreadable, refactor it back to a standard loop or break it down into smaller helper methods.
